packages.name: dash
packages.description: dash, a small POSIX shell; also /bin/sh
packages.title: Dash
packages.about: Dash is a small, fast POSIX shell, and Nova's /bin/sh: shell scripts with #!/bin/sh run with it. Nova's own shell, nsh, stays the Terminal's.

packages.name: dropbear
packages.description: Dropbear SSH: a server (dropbear), client (dbclient), scp and dropbearkey
packages.title: Dropbear SSH
packages.about: Log in to Nova from another computer, or from Nova to others: an SSH server (dropbear), a client (dbclient), scp to copy files, and dropbearkey to make keys. Logins are by key; docs/SSH.md tells how.

changes.notes: - Logs in as the user you name, with their own permissions, now that Nova has users (needs the Nova update published with it; the -1 build can't log in on it).
- Dropbear SSH: log in to Nova from another computer with a key (~/.ssh/authorized_keys), and copy files with scp.

packages.name: fonts-noto
packages.description: Noto fonts: Chinese, Japanese, Korean, many more scripts, symbols and color emoji
packages.title: Noto Fonts
packages.about: Fonts for the writing systems, symbols and emoji that Nova's own fonts don't have, so pages in Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Hebrew, Thai, Hindi and many more languages, and emoji, show up in the browser instead of empty boxes. Google's Noto family, under the SIL Open Font License.

changes.notes: - The first version: Chinese, Japanese and Korean, many other scripts, symbols, math and color emoji for the browser.

packages.name: kilo
packages.description: kilo, a small text editor for the terminal
packages.title: Kilo
packages.about: A small text editor that runs in the Terminal: kilo FILE. Ctrl+S saves, Ctrl+Q quits, Ctrl+F finds.

packages.name: ladybird
packages.description: A web browser with its own engine: today's web, JavaScript and all
packages.title: Ladybird
packages.about:
Ladybird is an independent web browser, written from scratch: its own HTML, CSS and JavaScript engines, so modern sites work, YouTube included.
It opens from Web in the dock, with tabs, an address bar, copy and paste. Each tab may use up to half the computer's memory; a page that runs away is closed alone.

changes.notes: - WebGL pages no longer close the tab on an NVIDIA card: the part of the browser that draws them stopped while setting up the card's memory.

- WebGL, for 3D on web pages (maps, games, product viewers), on GeForce RTX 30 and 40 cards: drawn by the card through ANGLE on Vulkan. Needs the NVIDIA Graphics package; without an NVIDIA card pages see no WebGL, as before.
- Leaving fullscreen on a YouTube video no longer closes the page ("Ladybird flew off-course"): a check in the browser's engine stopped it while the page was between styles.

- Real fullscreen: a video's fullscreen button (or a page asking for it) fills the whole screen, without the browser's tabs and toolbar or Nova's top bar and dock. Esc (or the video's button again) goes back. Needs the Nova update published with it.
- Pages with a lot to draw (YouTube) no longer stop the browser on an NVIDIA card: the graphics driver's way of counting finished GPU work was missing a piece it needed once enough had been drawn.
- Drawing on an NVIDIA card works: the browser stopped at start on one, since a Vulkan question only a loader answers went unanswered.

- With an NVIDIA RTX 30 or 40 card and the NVIDIA Graphics package, pages are drawn by the graphics card (Vulkan) instead of the processor. Without one nothing changes.
- If drawing on the card misbehaves, `touch /.config/web-no-gpu` in the Terminal keeps the browser on the processor (and `rm /.config/web-no-gpu` undoes it).

- "Open in New Tab" (and links that open a new tab) show the tab: before, the page loaded somewhere hidden.
- View Source works on big pages: their source is shown as plain text, in seconds instead of minutes.
- No crash when the browser is closed with the Downloads page open.

- Downloads work: they go into the new Downloads folder, and a notification says when each is done (or why it failed).
- A Downloads button in the toolbar (or Ctrl+J) lists them, with progress while they run and Open / Show in folder when done.
- "Download Linked File As..." asks where to save in Nova's Save window; screenshots from the page menu save the same way.

- Right-click menus: on a page (back, forward, reload, copy, paste, select all, view source), a link (open in a new tab, download, copy its address), an image (open, save, copy) and selected text (search the web). The address bar has cut, copy, paste and "Paste and Go"; a tab has new tab, reload and close.

- Emoji, symbols, math and every language's letters show on web pages: the browser now looks through all of Nova's fonts for a character the page's font lacks.
- Brings the new Noto Fonts package with it.
- The address bar edits like a text field: click to place the cursor, move it with the arrow keys, select with the mouse or Shift, and copy, cut and paste.
- Pages that start helper programs no longer fail.
- The first Ladybird for Nova.

packages.name: lua
packages.description: Lua 5.4, a small and fast scripting language
packages.title: Lua
packages.about: Lua is a small, fast scripting language, easy to learn and to embed. Run scripts with lua FILE, or type lua for its prompt.

packages.name: make
packages.description: GNU make 4.4.1, which builds programs from makefiles
packages.title: GNU Make
packages.about: make builds programs from makefiles, rebuilding only what changed. With Nova's C compiler (tcc) it builds C programs on Nova itself.

packages.name: micropython
packages.title: MicroPython
packages.about: A lean Python 3 that starts in an instant: micropython FILE.py runs a script. For the full language and its standard library, there is Python.

packages.name: nova
packages.description: Nova itself: the kernel and the system every app runs on
packages.title: Nova
packages.about:
Updates Nova on the disk it was installed on. The new version starts at the next restart; the one you have now stays in the boot menu as "Nova (previous version)", in case the new one misbehaves. Your apps, settings and files aren't touched.
A Nova running from a USB stick is updated by writing a new image to the stick.

changes.notes: - A renamed user's home follows their name at their next login
- People can be renamed: usermod -l and Settings' Rename
- Filesystem calls run with interrupts off; ext2 folders that got their parent's block are fixed
- Settings sets a first password: it asks for the current one only if there is one
- Server mode logs in before its console starts; fixes for CI
- Settings' Users pane: add people, change passwords, remove people
- Each user's own settings; the server console asks who logs in
- The login screen, the lock screen and Log Out
- The desktop runs apps as the user who logged in
- Accounts: /etc/passwd, Argon2id passwords, su, sudo, login and useradd
- Processes run as users: ids, setuid programs and permission checks
- Windows show what the app last flushed, not a half-drawn buffer
- Vulkan and OpenGL windows present at the desktop's real frames (SYS_FRAME_WAIT)
- mkpkg: notes are needed from a package's second revision, not for any version
- nvidia -16: flips off unless nvidia.flips=on, until they work on a real card
- A window made smaller than asked keeps a buffer of the size asked for at first
- Flips that don't finish fall back to drawing on the screen, and don't starve the system
- The desktop flips at the NVIDIA display's vblank: no more tearing
- OpenArena: the first game, on ioquake3 with SDL and OpenGL through Zink
- Pointer lock for games that steer with the mouse, and SDL's relative mode on it
- SDL 2 for Nova: its own video and audio drivers, and sdl2-demos
- nvidia-vulkan gets What's new notes; mkpkg wants them past -1
- EGL: Nova windows only on 8-bit configs
- libvulkan: RGBA swapchains, swapped into the window as it's copied
- publish: Nova isn't published again when only its version changed

- libvulkan: one lock for queue submissions
- publish: a published package is never replaced under the same version
- OpenGL in Nova windows: EGL window surfaces on Zink, and glcube
- NVK: the GPU address range it sees stops at 512 GiB, as with nouveau
- Modules run with interrupts off, so a driver lock can't freeze the PC
- Clock: a TSC measured below 100 MHz means the timer didn't count

packages.name: nvidia
packages.description: NVIDIA's open GPU driver, for GeForce RTX 30 and 40 cards
packages.title: NVIDIA Graphics
packages.about:
NVIDIA's open-source GPU driver, for GeForce RTX 30 and 40 series cards (RTX 3050 to 4090). Nova loads it when it starts, if it finds one of these cards, and writes what it found to /var/log/nvidia.log.
With it, the browser draws pages on the card, Settings > Display can let the card drive the screen (a trial until you keep it), Task Manager shows the card's activity in its GPU tab, and Vulkan programs (the NVIDIA Vulkan package has two to try) use it for 3D.
If Nova ever stops while starting it, the next start skips it by itself (and says so), until a new version comes. modules=off in /etc/nova.conf turns every driver from a package off.

changes.notes: - The screen no longer tears: each frame of the desktop is shown at the monitor's refresh, so moving windows, scrolling, games and video are smooth. (-14 and -15 tried this and left the screen black: a function the driver lacks was called; fixed.) nvidia.flips=off in /etc/nova.conf goes back to the old way.

- Back to drawing straight on the screen, as up to -13: the flips of -14 and -15 left the screen black on some cards. They're off until they're known to work; nvidia.flips=on in /etc/nova.conf tries them.

- Fixes -14's black screen at start: if the card doesn't take a flipped frame within a quarter of a second, the desktop goes back to drawing straight on the screen (it may tear, but it works), and the log says why. The desktop no longer keeps programs waiting while a frame is on its way. Needs the Nova update published with it.

- The screen no longer tears: the desktop draws each frame out of sight and the card shows it at the monitor's refresh, so moving windows, games and video are smooth, at the monitor's own rate. Needs the Nova update published with it.
- In the Store for everyone with a GeForce RTX 30 or 40 card: no testing source to add first. The description says what the driver does now.
- Task Manager gets a GPU tab: how busy the card is (drawing, memory, video decoding and encoding), its video memory and its performance state. Needs the Nova update published with it.
- Programs can map system memory the card uses (it was refused as "not supported"): Vulkan (NVIDIA Vulkan's vktest) needs it to start the card.
- Programs can map the card's memory (video memory and system memory it uses) and write to it directly, as graphics libraries do; nvidia-info checks it. Needs the Nova update published with it.
- When the monitor is switched off and on again (or its cable unplugged and plugged back in), the picture comes back: the mode is set again.

- Settings > Display's resolutions go down as well as up (they were listed biggest first).
- Switches on the card's own sound device for HDMI and DisplayPort, so Settings > Sound can play through your monitor or TV (needs the Nova update published with it).
- Fixes the black screen: the display's output scale was left at zero, which turns every pixel black.

- If the display setup fails partway, the screen is given back to the old display instead of staying black.
- The last start's log is kept as /var/log/nvidia.log.1, and the log says more about each display step.

- The display: NVIDIA's display driver sets your monitor to its own resolution and refresh rate, and Nova's desktop draws through the graphics card. Settings > Display lists the monitor's modes.
- The first time, it's a trial: press Keep in Settings > Display. If the screen stayed black and you couldn't, the next start goes back to the old display by itself.
- Needs the Nova update published with it.

- Programs can talk to the driver: /dev/nvidiactl and /dev/nvidia0, as on Linux. The nvidia-info command (in the Terminal) asks it for the card's name, memory and the driver's version. Needs the Nova update published with it.

- When the driver waits for something another part of it does (its interrupt work, queued work, timers), that work now runs while it waits, instead of the wait being skipped. Waits that never end are logged with where they were.
- The card's interrupts are connected (MSI): the driver's check that they arrive stopped it before. Needs the Nova update published with it.
- First test: finds the card, starts NVIDIA's driver and the card's firmware, and writes what happened to /var/log/nvidia.log.

packages.name: nvidia-vulkan
packages.description: Vulkan and OpenGL for NVIDIA cards (Mesa's NVK and Zink, Google's ANGLE): vktest, gltest and zinktest check the card, vkcube and glcube spin cubes
packages.title: NVIDIA Vulkan
packages.about:
Vulkan, the 3D and compute interface, for GeForce RTX 30 and 40 cards: Mesa's open NVK driver, on NVIDIA's driver (the NVIDIA Graphics package).
Two programs to try in the Terminal: vktest lists the card, runs a small program on it, draws a triangle and saves it as vktest.png in your home folder (its last line says VKTEST PASS or what failed); vkcube opens a window with a spinning cube the card draws, and prints its frame rate; gltest draws a triangle with OpenGL ES through ANGLE, as the browser's WebGL does, and saves it as gltest.png (GLTEST PASS or what failed); zinktest draws one with OpenGL 4 through Mesa's Zink, as ported programs do, and saves it as zinktest.png (ZINKTEST PASS or what failed); glcube spins a cube with OpenGL in a window you can resize (F11: fullscreen), and prints its frame rate.

changes.notes: - Vulkan and OpenGL windows (vkcube, glcube) show a frame each time the monitor refreshes, in step with the desktop, instead of every 15 ms: no more dropped frames. Needs the Nova update published with it.
- The Store shows what each version changed (this list).
- OpenGL windows use colors a window can show (8 bits a channel), so glcube's cube appears instead of a blank window.
- Vulkan windows take images in RGBA order too, as OpenGL (Zink) asks for them.
- Programs that use the card from several threads at once (OpenGL in a window does) no longer get in each other's way.

- OpenGL in windows: glcube spins a cube in a window you can resize (F11: fullscreen; glcube -i: as fast as it goes).
- Vulkan windows follow their window's size when it changes. Needs the Nova update published with it.
- zinktest finds its OpenGL settings on the card (it found none).
- OpenGL (Zink) starts on the card: it stopped with "out of host memory".
- OpenGL for ported programs, through Mesa's Zink on Vulkan: zinktest draws a triangle with OpenGL 4 and checks it.
- gltest sets up the card's memory as the browser does, so the browser's WebGL starts instead of crashing.
- OpenGL ES through Google's ANGLE, as the browser's WebGL uses it: gltest draws a triangle and checks it.

- vkcube and other Vulkan windows show a frame each time the desktop draws one, instead of hundreds nobody sees.
- vktest no longer ends with two error lines from the driver.
- Vulkan programs that wait for the card with timeline semaphores (the browser's drawing) work.
- Programs that ask Vulkan for layers (the browser does) get an answer.
- vkcube's frame rate lines appear as they're printed.
- vkcube draws the cube's front faces (it showed the inside).
- Vulkan for programs, with windows: vkcube spins a cube in a window and prints its frame rate.
- vktest's shaders compile for the card.
- When vktest fails, it shows what NVIDIA's driver said.
- Vulkan can use the computer's memory for the card, as NVIDIA's driver requires.
- The card is set up the way Mesa expects.
- Vulkan's functions are all in place in a program (some were missing).
- vktest says where Vulkan stopped when it fails.
- First test: vktest, Vulkan through Mesa's NVK on NVIDIA's driver. It lists the card, runs a small program on it, draws a triangle and saves it as vktest.png.

packages.name: openarena
packages.description: OpenArena: a fast first-person arena shooter against bots or online (ioquake3), for NVIDIA cards
packages.title: OpenArena
packages.about: A fast-paced first-person arena shooter in the style of the 1999 classics: run, jump and fight across arenas against bots, or join players on the internet. The engine is ioquake3; the game, its maps and its sounds are OpenArena's, all free software. Needs an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 30 or 40 card with the NVIDIA Graphics and NVIDIA Vulkan packages. The mouse aims (Alt+Tab gets it back); settings and saves are kept in your home folder's .local/share/openarena. openarena-server in the Terminal runs a server for others to join.

packages.name: python
packages.title: Python
packages.about: Python 3.14, the reference implementation (CPython), with its standard library: python3 FILE.py runs a script, python3 alone gives its prompt.

packages.name: sdl2-demos
packages.description: SDL 2's test programs: sprites, an OpenGL cube, a looping sound and a locked mouse, to try SDL on Nova
packages.title: SDL Demos
packages.about: Programs that try SDL, the library many games are built on, on Nova. In the Terminal: sdl2-testsprite draws smiley faces bouncing around a window (with OpenGL on an NVIDIA card, or without it); sdl2-testgl2 spins a coloured cube with OpenGL (needs the NVIDIA Graphics and NVIDIA Vulkan packages and a GeForce RTX 30 or 40 card); sdl2-loopwave plays a sound until you press Ctrl+C; sdl2-testrelative locks the mouse in its window, the way games that steer with it do, and moves a red square as you move the mouse (Alt+Tab lets go, Escape ends it).

changes.notes: - sdl2-testrelative: the mouse locked in the window, as games that steer with it use it (needs the Nova update published with it).
- First version: sdl2-testsprite, sdl2-testgl2 and sdl2-loopwave, SDL's own test programs on Nova.

packages.name: yipyap-server
packages.description: Run your own Discord-style chat server, with a web client for any browser
packages.title: YipYap Server
packages.about:
YipYap is a chat server you run yourself: hubs with public and private spaces, direct and group chats, threads, reactions, file sharing, search, invites and roles, voice and video calls between browsers, and a soundboard. Profiles have pictures (animated ones too) and banners, the web client installs as an app, and it can send notifications while it's closed.
Open YipYap Server to start it: it shows the address to give the people on your network (http://THIS-COMPUTER:7777), and can start with Nova. It always uses HTTPS, which calls need: the server makes its own certificate the first time it starts, and the app shows its fingerprint to compare when you connect. The first account made becomes the administrator. Messages and files are kept in /var/lib/yipyap.

changes.notes:
- Coming back to the app on a phone reconnects straight away, instead of waiting a while for messages to catch up.
- A test notification the phone's notification service accepted is noted in the server's log.
- Server settings can go in /var/lib/yipyap/yipyap.db.conf, one per line (for example "push-contact mailto:you@example.org"), since the app starts the server without options.

- A new device (or the app installed again) starts with old messages read, instead of showing the whole history as unread.
- When a phone's notification service refuses a notification, the server's log says why.

- What you've read is kept on the server, so your phone and computer agree on what's unread.
- iPhone no longer zooms into text fields (which left the page zoomed and shifted).
- The notification test waits six seconds, so you can leave the app and see it arrive.

- The server runs as a Nova service: if it ever crashes, Nova starts it again by itself, and its log keeps the time of every line (needs Nova 2026.10.27 or newer).
- "Start with Nova" moves over to Nova's services by itself the first time you open the app.
- On iPhone, the page no longer scrolls behind menus and drawers, and side panels stay clear of the status bar and the home bar.

- Profiles: a picture (animated ones play on hover) and a banner, with a card and an editor that crops them.
- The web client installs as an app, and works offline as far as it can.
- Notifications while YipYap is closed (Web Push), also on Nova.
- Open in browser works again with a certificate made by an older version: one that doesn't name 127.0.0.1 or this computer's address is made again at start.
- An address typed without https:// still opens the chat: plain HTTP is sent on to HTTPS.
- HTTPS works in Nova's own browser at 127.0.0.1.
- Call tiles are centered; close buttons and icons are easier to see.
- Call audio fixed.
- Big files arrive whole over HTTPS.
- HTTPS with no setup.
- HTTPS with a certificate made on Nova.
